name: Jewish Autonomism
summary: Jewish Autonomism, Simon Dubnow's doctrine, holds that the Jews are a living nation of a spiritual, cultural-historical kind that survived the loss of state, land and common language, and that in the Diaspora they should seek not a territory of their own but national-cultural autonomy inside the multinational states where they live. Its chief axiom is that Jews hold all citizens' rights both as individuals and as members of their nationality: secular, democratically run communities, their own schools and freedom of language, together with full civic and political equality. It rejects assimilation as national suicide and political Zionism's state as a messianic fantasy, while welcoming Palestine as one spiritual centre, puts national politics above class politics, and ties Jewish emancipation to a democratic constitutional order.
scope: Simon Dubnow's autonomism, which the Encyclopaedia Judaica (s2) says he named in 1901 and Pinson's essay (s7) presents as his national theory: the Letters on Old and New Judaism (1897-1907), including the Folkspartei programme he set out in the Twelfth Letter, read in the English edition Nationalism and History (s6), and his later programmatic letter of 1939 (s8). The Bund's socialist version, the Sejmists, Austro-Marxist personal autonomy, American diaspora nationalism (Janowsky, Kallen) and the Folkspartei's later Polish and Baltic branches are other subjects and are not used; nor is the unrelated autonomist Marxism.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-10), bringing a pre-rules audit up to rules 5. The first pass rested on Wikipedia and two short encyclopedia entries; this pass read Dubnow's own Letters on Old and New Judaism in full English translation (Nationalism and History, archive.org), his 1939 letter and Pinson's introductory essay, and rewrote or nulled every earlier answer (reviewHistory keeps them); the three earlier missing statements, already added to the bank, are now cited to the Letters and Pinson, which state them. Earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia, on autonomism's general aims or on what adherents would probably think were nulled (159). Themes searched in the full text: government (democracy, constitution, parties, parliament, rule of law, autonomy and its guarantees), liberty and rights (equal rights, group rights, language, schools), society and culture (religion and secularism, assimilation, tradition, education, continuity), means (revolution, self-defence, gradualism, organisation), world (Zionism, Palestine, emigration, expansionism, militarism, totalitarianism), and economy (class struggle, unions, socialism, property, trade), where the Letters say little beyond rejecting class politics; ecology, technology, gender and family, crime and most economic policy are not discussed at all. Not reached: the YIVO Encyclopedia articles (a script-only page that returns no text) and Gechtman's article on Érudit (bot check). The Encyclopaedia Judaica entries on Autonomism, Dubnow and the Folkspartei (s2, s4 and encyclopedia.com's Folkspartei entry) were read but are not cited for current answers: they call the doctrine 'Autonomism', which in this catalog is the name of a different ideology, so the source check cannot tie them to Jewish Autonomism by name. Over time: Dubnow grew more receptive to Palestine (the 1937 preface says he opposed only Zionism's denial of the Diaspora); answers follow the Letters, his mature statement. Contested points: he rejects class politics but accepts workers' economic struggle (class-collaboration 0), demands all rights at once yet works step by step (gradual-change, small-step-social-reform 0), ranks national types by stage while affirming the equal worth of nations (cultures-equal-different 0), and declined to make Hebrew the Diaspora's language while welcoming its revival in Palestine (revive-national-language 0).
